<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
It is clear that $\mathcal{C}_theta^* = \mathcal{C}_theta$. In general, $\Sigma^*$ is not a convex capillary hypersurface.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- conj-1: body_md -->
\cite{MWW25}
Let $theta in  (0, \frac{pi}{2})$ and $\Sigma$ be an even, smooth, strictly convex capillary hypersurface. Then
\begin{equation}\label{conj}
\operatorname{vol}(\widehat{\Sigma}) \operatorname{vol}(\widehat{\Sigma^*}) \leq \operatorname{vol}(\widehat{\mathcal{C}_theta})^2.
\end{equation}
Moreover, equality holds if and only if $\Sigma = \lambda \mathcal{C}_theta$ for some $\lambda > 0$.
<!-- end conj-1 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm 1}
Let $theta in  \left(0, \frac{pi}{2}\right)$. For any unconditional convex body $K$ (not necessarily smooth or capillary) with the standard support function $h_K$ we have
\begin{equation}
\frac{\operatorname{vol}(K)}{2n} 
\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}_theta} 
\frac{(1 - \costheta \, x_n)^{n+1}}{h_K^n(x)} \, d\sigma(x) 
\leq \operatorname{vol}(\widehat{\mathcal{C}_theta})^2.
\end{equation}
In particular, when $\Sigma$ is an unconditional, smooth, strictly convex capillary hypersurface, we have
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{vol}(\widehat{\Sigma}) 
\operatorname{vol}(\widehat{\Sigma^*}) 
\leq \operatorname{vol}(\widehat{\mathcal{C}_theta})^2.
\end{equation}
Moreover, equality holds if and only if 
$\Sigma = \lambda \mathcal{C}_theta$ for some $\lambda > 0$.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm 2}
Let $theta in  \left(0, \frac{pi}{2}\right)$ and let $f in  C^2(\mathcal{C}_theta)$ be an unconditional function satisfying $\bar{\nabla}_\mu f = 0$, where $\mu$ denotes the unit normal vector to $\partial \mathcal{C}_theta \subset \mathcal{C}_theta$ pointing towards the lower half-space. Then
\begin{equation}
\int_{\mathcal{C}_theta} f \left( \Delta_{\mathcal{C}_theta} f + 2n f \right) \, dV_{\mathcal{C}_theta} \leq 2n \frac{\left( \int_{\mathcal{C}_theta} f \, dV_{\mathcal{C}_theta} \right)^2}{\int_{\mathcal{C}_theta} dV_{\mathcal{C}_theta}}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem 1} The function
 $x\mapsto V(\sqrt{x})$ is concave in $(0,\infty)^n$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $s=x_1+\cdots+x_{n-1}$ and $x_n=t$. Define
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
v(s,t)=V(\sqrt{x})=\frac{1}{2\sin^4theta}\left((1+\cos^2theta)t+(\sin^2theta)s +2\costheta \sqrt{t^2+s t\sin^2theta}\right).
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
Then the Hessian of $v$ (a function of two variables $s,t$) is
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
D^2v=\begin{bmatrix}
v_{ss} & v_{st}\\
v_{ts} & v_{tt}
\end{bmatrix}=-\frac{\costheta}{4(t^2+s t\sin^2theta)^\frac{3}{2}}\begin{bmatrix}
    t^2 & -st \\
    -st & s^2
\end{bmatrix}.
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
From this we obtain
\begin{equation}
D^2V(\sqrt{x}) = -\frac{\costheta}{4(t^2+s t\sin^2theta)^\frac{3}{2}}
\begin{bmatrix}
t^2 & \cdots & t^2 & -st \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
t^2 & \cdots & t^2 & -st \\
-st& \cdots & -st & s^2
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Recall $thetain  (0,\frac{pi}{2})$. Then for any $a=(a_1,\ldots, a_n)in  \mathbb{R}^n$, there holds
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
D^2V(\sqrt{x})(a,a)=-\frac{\costheta}{4(t^2+s t\sin^2theta)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\big(t\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}a_i-sa_n\big)^2 \leq 0.
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem 2}
The function $V^{\ast}$ is of class $C^1$, and for $y=(y',y_n)$ satisfying $|y_n| \leq |y| \cos theta$, we have
\begin{equation}
DV^{\ast}(y) = \sin^2 theta \, (y', 0).
\end{equation}
Moreover, we have
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
\det D^2V^{\ast}(y) =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } |y_n| < |y| \cos theta , \\
(1-\frac{|y_n|}{|y|}\costheta)^{n+1} & \text{if } |y_n| > |y| \cos theta.
\end{cases}
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
In particular, the Monge-Amp\`ere measure of $V^{\ast}$ is
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
\mu_{V^{\ast}}(A)=\int_{A\cap\{y:\, |y_n|>|y|\costheta \}}\(1-\frac{|y_n|}{|y|}\costheta\)^{n+1}\, dy,
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
for any Borel set $A$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Since $C$ is strictly convex, by \cite[Cor. 1.7.3]{Schneider}, $h_C$ is differentiable at $y \neq 0$. Since $V^{\ast}$ is two-homogeneous, we have $DV^{\ast}(0) = 0$. Moreover, a convex differentiable function on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $C^1$; see \cite[Thm. 1.5.4]{Schneider}.

The second claim follows from a well-known identity: a smooth, strictly convex hypersurface with support function $h$ and Gauss curvature $\mathcal{K}$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
\det D^2\frac{1}{2}h^2(x)=\frac{h^{n+1}}{\mathcal{K}}\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right).
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
Here the Gauss curvature is regarded as a function on the unit sphere via the Gauss map. See, for instance, \cite[Thm. 3.1]{MP14}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem 3}Let $A=(0,\infty)^n$ and $B=\{ y in  (0,\infty)^n :\, y_n> |y|\costheta \}$. Then $ D V(A) =B$, $DV: A\to B$ is a $C^{\infty}$ diffeomorphism and
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
\det D^2V(x)\det D^2V^{\ast}(DV(x))=1\quad \forall xin  A.
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $r=\sqrt{x_n^2+|x'|^2\sin^2theta}$ and define $\phiin  (0,\frac{pi}{2})$ through $\cos \phi=\frac{x_n}{r}$ and $\sin \phi=\frac{\sintheta |x'|}{r}$. Let $y=(y',y_n)=DV(x)$. Then
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
y_n&=\frac{r}{\sin^4theta}(1+\costheta \cos\phi)(\costheta+\cos\phi),\\
y'&=\frac{1+\costheta\cos\phi}{\sin^2theta}x',\quad |y'|=\frac{r}{\sin^3theta}(1+\costheta\cos\phi)\sin\phi.
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}

Define $f(\phi)=\frac{\sintheta \sin\phi}{\costheta+\cos\phi}=\frac{|y'|}{y_n}$ for $\phiin  (0,\frac{pi}{2})$. Since $f$ is strictly increasing and maps $(0,\frac{pi}{2})$ onto $(0,\tantheta)$, we have $0<|y'|/y_n<\tantheta$, which is equivalent to $y_n>|y|\costheta$. Hence $DV(A)\subset B$.

Let $yin  B$. We choose $\phiin (0,\frac{pi}{2})$ such that $f(\phi)=|y'|/y_n$, and define
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
r=\frac{\sin^4theta\, y_n}{(1+\costheta\cos\phi)(\costheta+\cos\phi)}.
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
x=r\left(\frac{\sin\phi}{\sintheta}\frac{y'}{|y'|},\cos\phi\right)in  A \quad \text{and} \quad  DV(x)=y.
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
Hence $B\subset DV(A)$.

Note that $V=\frac{1}{2}p_C^2$ is $C^\infty$-smooth and strictly convex on the open set $A$, and thus the gradient map $DV: A \to B$ is bijective. By the inverse function theorem, since $D^2 V(x)$ is positive definite for $x in  A$, the map $DV$ is a diffeomorphism. Moreover, from the definition of the Legendre transform, for $y in  B$, we have $DV^{\ast}(y) = x$, where $x in  A$ satisfies $y = DV(x)$. Thus, $DV^{\ast}(DV(x))=x$ and the relation between the determinants follows.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\cite{Pre71,Lei72,Bor75,Dub77}
Let $\lambda in  (0, 1)$ and let $f$, $g$ and $h$ be non-negative integrable functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Assume that
\[
h((1 - \lambda)x + \lambda y) \geq f(x)^{1-\lambda} g(y)^{\lambda}
\]
for all $x, y in  \mathbb{R}^n$. Then
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} h  \geq \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f \right)^{1-\lambda} \left( \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} g  \right)^{\lambda}.
\]
If $f$ and $g$ have positive integrals and equality holds, then there exist $a > 0$, $w in  \mathbb{R}^n$, and a log-concave function $\tilde{h}$, such that $h = \tilde{h}$, $f(x) = a^{\lambda} \tilde{h}(x +\lambda w)$, and $g(x) = a^{ -(1-\lambda)} \tilde{h}(x -(1- \lambda) w)$ for almost every $x$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
Let $A=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ with $a_i>0$. If $A\mathcal{C}_{theta}$ is $theta$-capillary, then for all $i$ we have $a_i=a_n$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $x in  \mathbb{S}^{n-1}_{theta}$. The outer unit  normal to $A \mathbb{S}^{n-1}_{theta}$ at $Ax$ is given by
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
    \nu(x) = \frac{A^{-1}x}{|A^{-1}x|},
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
and we have
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
    \langle \nu(x), E_n \rangle 
    = \frac{x_n}{a_n\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n \tfrac{x_i^2}{a_i^2}}}.
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
In particular, for $i=1,\ldots,n-1$, the point $e_i = \sintheta\, E_i + \costheta\, E_n in  \partial \mathbb{S}^{n-1}_{theta}$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
    \langle \nu(e_i), E_n \rangle
    = \frac{\costheta}{\sqrt{\cos^2theta + \tfrac{a_n^2}{a_i^2}\sin^2theta}}.
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
If $A \mathcal{C}_{theta}$ is $theta$-capillary, then there holds
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
    \cos^2theta + \frac{a_n^2}{a_i^2}\sin^2theta = 1, \quad i=1,\ldots,n-1.
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
Hence, $a_i = a_n$ for all $i$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor 1}Let $\alpha in  (-n, 0)$. For an unconditional convex body $K$ define
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
\mathcal{E}_\alpha(K) = \int_{\mathbb{S}_{theta}^{n-1}} \left( \frac{h_K}{h_C} \right)^\alpha h_C\, d\sigma.
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
If $\operatorname{vol}(K) = \operatorname{vol}(C)$, then
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
\mathcal{E}_\alpha(K) \leq \mathcal{E}_\alpha(C) &= \int_{\mathbb{S}_{theta}^{n-1}} h_C\, d\sigma, \\
\int_{\mathbb{S}_{theta}^{n-1}} h_C \log h_K\, d\sigma &\geq \int_{\mathbb{S}_{theta}^{n-1}} h_C \log h_C\, d\sigma.
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
Moreover, equality holds only when $K = C$.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The inequalities follow from Jensen's inequality and \eqref{ineq x}. If equality holds in either inequality, then equality must also hold in Jensen's inequality, and therefore $h_K/h_C$ is constant on $\mathbb{S}^{n-1}_theta$ and hence $K=C$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
We construct a family of $C^{1,1}$-smooth convex bodies that are smooth near $x_{n} = 0$ and meet this hyperplane at the constant angle $theta in  (\frac{pi}{2}, pi)$.  In this example, we write points in $\mathbb{R}^n$ in the form
$(x,y)$ with $xin \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ and $yin \mathbb{R}$. For $\lambda > 0$, define
\[
\begin{aligned}
K_{\lambda} &\coloneqq \left\{ (x, y) in  \frac{1}{\lambda} \widehat{\mathcal{C}_theta} : y \leq -\frac{\cos theta}{\lambda} \right\} \\
&\quad \cup \left\{ (x, y) in  \mathbb{R}^n : |x| \leq \frac{1}{\lambda}, -\frac{\cos theta}{\lambda} \leq y \leq \lambda^{n-1} \right\} \cup \left( \frac{1}{\lambda} B^n + \lambda^{n-1} E_n \right).
\end{aligned}
\]
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
We consider the intersection of an ellipse and the half-space $y\geq 0$ given by:
\begin{equation}\begin{alignedat}{2} 
K= \left\{(x,y): \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{(y - c)^2}{b^2} \leq 1, \quad y \geq 0\right\},
 \end{alignedat}\end{equation}
where $a > 0$, $b > c > 0$ are constants to be determined later. Let us put $\Sigma=\overline{\partial K\cap \mathbb{R}^2_+}$. Suppose the contact angle of $\Sigma$ with $y=0$ is $thetain  (\frac{pi}{2},pi)$.
<!-- end head-2 -->
